transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-10-14
Start: 16:00 PDT
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Lina Park (Redwood AE), Omar Ruiz (Redwood SE), Priya Shah (Redwood Product), Marcus Lee (CTO - Aurora), Sasha Kim (Head of ML - Aurora), Ava Patel (Eng Manager - Aurora)

[00:00] Lina: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we really appreciate the time. quick intro, I'm Lina - i'll run through the agenda and Omar will do the deep tech demo.
[00:08] Marcus: thanks Lina, appreciate it. we got a bunch of questions specifically around structured output and how we can call internal tools safely.
[00:15] Omar: cool, yep that's exactly what we wanted to show — JSON mode, schemas, and function/tool calling with guardrails. i'll share my screen in a sec. bear with me, screen is starting.
[00:30] Omar: okay, so at a high level Redwood supports two main approaches: free-form generation and structured output via JSON mode. for product use cases where downstream systems ingest output, we recommend schema enforcement.
[00:44] Sasha: quick question — how strict is the schema enforcement? can we allow optional fields or have versioned schemas?
[00:52] Omar: yes, you can declare a JSON schema in the request or save schemas in the Console. Redwood will validate the model output against the schema; mismatches can be rejected, or you can configure a fallback that returns a best-effort parse plus a validation error tag. versioning is supported via schema ids in the model config.
[01:10] Ava: any examples?
[01:13] Omar: absolutely. demo time — i'm going to switch to our Console. (pause) alright in the Console -> API Playground we have a 'JSON mode' toggle. i set the schema: {"type":"object","properties":{"customer_id":{"type":"string"},"intent":{"type":"string"},"entities":{"type":"array"}},"required":["customer_id","intent"]}. now i call the hosted endpoint with function-calling enabled — note the response comes in a structured payload, and there's a top-level _validation object when anything is off.
[01:46] Marcus: the validation object... does that include line-level errors or just a pass/fail?
[01:51] Omar: it's pretty granular, you get field-level errors, expected vs got, and a confidence score for model-chosen fields. you can hook these to your error handling to trigger retries, fallback models, or human review.
[02:08] Sasha: and for function calling — can it call our internal microservices or only pre-defined actions?
[02:14] Omar: function calling is agnostic — you register a schema for the function and a mapping to an http webhook or internal tool. the Console supports short-circuiting via a verify step: first Redwood will return the proposed function call JSON, then you can choose to auto-execute or route to a service. many customers use a 'dry-run' mode to inspect calls before execution.
[02:38] Ava: how do you prevent the model from hallucinating calls or calling unauthorized endpoints?
[02:42] Omar: good question — we have guardrails at multiple layers: schema enforcement for structure, domain whitelists for allowed functions/endpoints, and runtime RBAC so only signed, approved functions are executable. we also log every call in the audit trail.
[02:58] Lina: i'll jump in here — on enterprise plans we provide SSO/SAML, RBAC and KMS integration for encryption at rest. Omar will share the SOC2 artifacts in the pack.
[03:08] Marcus: awesome. another thing — latency requirements: some of our pathways require sub-150ms token latency. can you talk about dedicated vs hosted and options for low-latency?
[03:18] Omar: sure. for sub-150ms you usually need a dedicated flavor and pinned model/instance placement. Redwood Dedicated gives reserved GPU pools and region pinning; for the hosted API we provide performance profiles, and Optimize suggests batching and quantization configs but those can add latency. for really tight SLOs we do co-located private deployments or dedicated instances.
[03:40] Sasha: what about cost tradeoffs? quantization often helps cost but might impact quality.
[03:46] Omar: yes, Optimize analyzes your prompts and recommends quantization levels per model and per route, plus batching windows that balance P99 latency vs tokens/sec. we can show example tradeoff curves from similar customers.
[03:58] Lina: i'm going to demo a quick flow where the model extracts structured fields, calls a function to enrich the user profile, and returns result. so first the model produces the call JSON...
[04:08] Omar: (typing) here's a sample response — note the 'function_call' block returned with name: enrich_profile and arguments as a JSON object. in the Console i have set a whitelist for that function so it maps to a secure webhook behind a private tunnel.
[04:24] Ava: do you support HMAC verification for webhooks?
[04:27] Omar: yes, we support HMAC signatures, mTLS, or signed tokens depending on your infra. and for Private deployments you can keep traffic inside the VPC.
[04:36] Marcus: for logging, can we redact PII before it hits logs?
[04:40] Priya: great point — we have pipeline hooks to redact or hash sensitive fields at ingestion time, and you can disable transcript logging for specific routes. logs can be forwarded to your SIEM and we also support retention policies per workspace.
[04:56] Sasha: curious about developer ergonomics — how easy is it to iterate on schemas and tests?
[05:01] Omar: Console has a schema registry and test harness. you can run a suite of prompt-driven tests and get diffed outputs. we also integrate with CI: push a schema update and the rollout system can do canary checks against a test set before updating production routes.
[05:20] Marcus: procurement and legal will want to see data residency and encryption details. Lina, will you send the security pack?
[05:26] Lina: yes, i'll send SOC2, encryption/KMS notes, and an overview of Private deployment options.
[05:31] Omar: i'll attach a sample benchmark script that you can run to test latency with your payloads. it supports both hosted and Dedicated endpoints and will output p50/p95/p99 and cost estimates.
[05:43] Ava: perfect. one more Q — how do you handle schema evolution in the field without breaking downstream systems?
[05:49] Omar: we recommend versioned schemas and a compatibility mode. Redwood's router can map old schema versions to transformations or run an adapter function. also you can configure deprecation warnings that surface in the Console during rollout.
[06:05] Marcus: are there any customers using this pattern in production?
[06:08] Lina: yes — a couple of retailers and a fintech are using structured output plus function calling to power transaction enrichment and routing. we can share anonymized case studies.
[06:17] Sasha: ok if we run a pilot — what's the minimum scope?
[06:20] Lina: typically 2-4 routes, a small test corpus (2k-10k calls) and a week of benchmarks to validate latency and cost. after that we can decide on Dedicated or Private.
[06:31] Marcus: timeline-wise procurement might take 3-6 weeks. we'd like to start the pilot mid-late October if possible.
[06:38] Lina: we can accommodate that. next steps i'll send pricing and a pilot contract template. Omar will send security docs and the benchmark script.
[06:46] Sasha: can you include an example of guardrail logs — like when the model tried to return unallowed data?
[06:51] Omar: yes i'll include sample audit logs and the Console view of validation failures.
[06:55] Ava: will the Console show token-level cost for routes?
[06:58] Priya: yes, Console has per-route cost breakdowns, token counts, and suggestions from Optimize for batching/quantization.
[07:06] Lina: cool — any final questions?
[07:09] Marcus: nothing else. thanks all.
[07:12] Lina: thanks everyone — we'll follow up with the pack and schedule.
